extracted.intended_audience: USPTO examiners and patent practitioners (applicants, attorneys, agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating patent claims for obviousness under 35 U.S.C. §103: identifies categories of changes that are prima facie obvious, factors for range and species claims, when routine optimization applies, how to establish and rebut a prima facie case, and how to treat art-recognized equivalence and suitability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changes in Shape
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere configuration or shape of a claimed device is a matter of choice and is prima facie obvious unless there is persuasive evidence that the particular configuration is significant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: In re Dailey — configuration of a disposable plastic nursing container was held to be a matter of choice; applicant must show new or unexpected results attributable to the configuration to overcome obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changes in Sequence of Adding Ingredients
rubrics_metrics.description: Reversing or changing the order of process steps or the sequence of mixing ingredients is prima facie obvious unless new or unexpected results are produced by the different sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Ex parte Rubin — reversing order of coating and impregnating steps rendered claims prima facie obvious. See also In re Burhans and In re Gibson. Selection of any order of performing process steps is prima facie obvious absent new/unexpected results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making Portable
rubrics_metrics.description: Claiming a device is portable or movable does not by itself patentably distinguish it from otherwise old devices unless the portability produces new or unexpected results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: In re Lindberg — portability alone insufficient; must show new or unexpected results attributable to portability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making Integral (one-piece construction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Converting multi-piece structures to an integral (one-piece) construction is often a matter of obvious engineering choice and prima facie obvious unless the one-piece structure achieves new/unexpected results or demonstrates insight contrary to the art's expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: In re Larson — one-piece brake drum was an obvious engineering choice. Counterexample: Schenck v. Nortron Corp. — one-piece gapless support eliminated a known problem (damping) and was held patentable because it showed unexpected insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making Separable (removability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Making parts separable or removable where access or desirability would motivate removal is prima facie obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: In re Dulberg — converting a press-fitted cap to a removable cap was obvious if access would be desirable for the worker in the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making Adjustable
rubrics_metrics.description: Substituting adjustable elements where the art recognizes a need for adjustment is not a patentable advance and is prima facie obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: In re Stevens — adding an adjustable finger hook or universal joint where adjustment was art-recognized was obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making Continuous
rubrics_metrics.description: Claiming continuous operation where the prior art discloses a batch process is prima facie obvious if the continuous step would have been obvious to one skilled in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: In re Dilnot — introducing foam continuously into a slurry was held obvious over batch process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversal of Parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Simply reversing the relative positions or movements of parts in a device is prima facie obvious when it does not change the operation in a meaningful way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: In re Gazda — making the clock move with the steering wheel rather than fixed to the column was an obvious modification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duplication of Parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere duplication of parts in a structure has no patentable significance unless the duplication produces a new and unexpected result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: In re Harza — adding multiple ribs where prior art showed a single-plus-shaped stop was not patentable absent new/unexpected function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rearrangement of Parts
rubrics_metrics.description: Rearranging parts (placement changes) is generally an obvious matter of design choice unless the prior art provides motivation or reason for a worker to make the specific rearrangement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: In re Japikse, In re Kuhle. Note: Ex parte Chicago Rawhide — mere ability to rearrange parts is not enough; prior art must provide motivation to make that specific change without benefit of applicant’s specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purifying an Old Product
rubrics_metrics.description: A purer form of a known material may be novel, but mere purity alone does not render a product unobvious; patentability depends on factors such as whether the purified form has the same utility and whether the prior art suggests the particular form or methods of obtaining it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors: (1) whether the claimed purified compound/composition has the same utility as prior art materials; (2) whether prior art suggests the claimed form or means to obtain it. Example: In re Cofer (crystalline form unobvious where prior art did not suggest crystals). Note: product-by-process — improving a process to increase purity does not create patentability if the product lacks structural or functional difference (e.g., Purdue Pharma v. Epic Pharma). See MPEP § 2113 and Ex parte Stern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overlapping, Approaching, and Similar Ranges — prima facie obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: If claimed ranges, amounts, or proportions overlap or lie inside ranges disclosed by the prior art, a prima facie case of obviousness exists; ranges that are merely close (approaching) may also create a prima facie case if a skilled person would expect similar properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: In re Wertheim, In re Woodruff (overlap of 'about 1-5%' and '>5%'), Titanium Metals Corp. v. Banner (very close alloy proportions deemed prima facie obvious). A prior art range that is extremely broad may present genus/species issues—see MPEP § 2144.08. Multiple prior art references together can supply a 'range' (Iron Grip Barbell). Cases and citations include Peterson, Harris, Baird, Jones, and others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation to Optimize Result-Effective Variables ('obvious to try')
rubrics_metrics.description: A parameter must be recognized as a result-effective variable before optimizing it can be characterized as routine; after KSR, 'obvious to try' can support obviousness when there is a design need or market demand and a finite number of predictable solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In re Antonie: need to recognize the parameter as result-effective. KSR: when design need/market demand and finite, predictable solutions exist, pursuing known options that lead to anticipated success can support obviousness. The presence of a known result-effective variable is one motivation factor but not the only one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Routine Optimization
rubrics_metrics.description: Optimizing within prior art conditions or discovering the optimum/workable ranges by routine experimentation is not inventive where the prior art discloses the relevant conditions, unless evidence shows the claimed concentration/temperature/etc. is critical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General principle: mere differences in concentration or temperature typically will not support patentability absent evidence of criticality. Examples: In re Aller, Peterson, In re Hoeschele, Merck v. Biocraft, In re Kulling, In re Geisler. History: changes in form, proportions, or degree generally do not sustain a patent absent criticality or unexpected results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebuttal — Showing That the Range Is Critical
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants can rebut a prima facie obviousness case by showing the claimed range is critical, typically by demonstrating unexpected results relative to the prior art range.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite In re Woodruff and cases requiring the applicant to establish criticality by proper factual showing (e.g., Minerals Separation v. Hyde; In re Scherl; In re Becket; In re Lilienfeld; In re Wells). See MPEP § 716.02 - § 716.02(g) for criticality and unexpected results discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebuttal — Showing That the Prior Art Teaches Away
rubrics_metrics.description: A prima facie case of obviousness may be rebutted by showing that the prior art, in any material respect, teaches away from the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: In re Geisler (Zehender did not teach away because it encouraged exploring thinner coatings). Applicant may also rely on substantial secondary considerations (commercial success, long-felt need, copying) to rebut, but must show nexus and adequate evidence (Iron Grip Barbell discussion of why offered evidence failed). See MPEP § 2145 X.D for 'teaching away' discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art-Recognized Equivalence — Combining Equivalents Known for Same Purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: It is prima facie obvious to combine two compositions or components when the prior art teaches each as useful for the same purpose and the combination flows logically from their individual teachings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: In re Kerkhoven — combining two conventional spray-dried detergents was prima facie obvious. Other examples: In re Crockett; Ex parte Quadranti (mixture of two known herbicides). The logical flow from individual teachings supports obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art-Recognized Equivalence — Substituting Equivalents Known for Same Purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Substituting one component for an art-recognized equivalent for the same purpose can support an obviousness rejection, but equivalency must be recognized in the prior art and not based solely on applicant’s disclosure or mere functional equivalence (e.g., Markush grouping).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: In re Ruff (Markush listing insufficient to establish equivalency); Smith v. Hayashi (both phthalocyanine and selenium were known photoconductors — supports substitution). An express suggestion to substitute is not necessary (In re Fout). The Office should rely on evidence that the equivalency was recognized in the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art-Recognized Suitability for an Intended Purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Selecting a known material from a list because it is suitable for a known intended purpose supports a prima facie obviousness determination — 'reading a list and selecting a known compound to meet known requirements is no more ingenious than selecting the last piece to put in the last opening in a jigsaw puzzle.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Sinclair & Carroll Co. v. Interchemical Corp. — selecting a solvent with known boiling point/vapor pressure characteristics for a printing ink was held obvious. See also In re Leshin and Ryco v. Ag-Bag Corp. for similar principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness of Species When Prior Art Teaches a Genus — general approach
rubrics_metrics.description: When a prior art reference discloses a genus that encompasses the claimed species or subgenus but does not expressly disclose the species, examiners should attempt to find additional prior art and, if not found, analyze whether the species would have been obvious to one of ordinary skill considering multiple factors rather than per se rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The fact that a claimed species falls within a disclosed genus is not by itself sufficient to establish prima facie obviousness (In re Baird; In re Jones). Office personnel must analyze the totality of circumstances and avoid per se rules (In re Brouwer; In re Ochiai). See MPEP § 2144.08 for further guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness of Species — Graham three-step process and required findings
rubrics_metrics.description: To establish a prima facie case of obviousness for species under a genus disclosure, apply the Graham factors: (A) determine scope and contents of the prior art; (B) ascertain differences between the prior art and claims; (C) determine level of ordinary skill in the art; and (D) evaluate evidence of secondary considerations. If prima facie made, burden shifts to applicant to rebut.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific examiner actions: 1) determine scope/content of relevant prior art and whether references qualify under 35 U.S.C. 102 and are analogous; 2) for a prior art genus, make findings on (A) genus structure and any species described, (B) physical/chemical properties/utilities and suggested limitations/problems addressed, (C) predictability of the technology, and (D) number of species encompassed by the genus; 3) identify and compare the closest disclosed prior art species/subgenus and make explicit findings on similarities/differences in structure, properties, and utilities; 4) evaluate level of ordinary skill in the art from the prior art standpoint and any applicant evidence; 5) determine whether one of ordinary skill would have been motivated to select the claimed species/subgenus. Case citations: Graham v. John Deere; In re Bell; In re Rijckaert; In re Oetiker; Stratoflex; In re Dillon.
